questions.title: 1) Ideal diodes: conduction state and node voltage
questions.promptHtml:
Use this diagram as your wiring reference. Click the Original drawing in the sidebar to enlarge it. For build tasks, connect the editable parts yourself and submit your own completed circuit and test results.

In each circuit (a), (b), and (c), node v is fed from +3 V and returns to ground through the elements shown. The diodes are ideal: a short circuit when ON and an open circuit when OFF.

  1. Determine whether each diode conducts.
  2. Find v and the current I.

Take I as the current flowing from the +3 V supply down toward ground (0 if no current flows).

Show your work: Show calculations and reasoning on solution pages or in notes. Final answers alone earn zero credit. For practical tasks include your completed schematic, breadboard, probe locations, readings with units, and a prediction-versus-test comparison. Use simulated supplies only. State any AI or automated-build assistance used; follow the instructor’s course policy.
hints: Assume a state, solve, then check: an ON diode needs i_D ≥ 0; an OFF diode needs v_D ≤ 0.
In (b) and (c), check which terminal of the diode is the anode.
checklist: State the assumed diode state for each circuit.
Verify it with i_D ≥ 0 or v_D ≤ 0.
Report v and I with units.

questions.title: 2(a) Two diodes, constant-drop model (R_top = 15 kΩ) · Design, build & test
questions.promptHtml:
Use this diagram as your wiring reference. Click the Original drawing in the sidebar to enlarge it. For build tasks, connect the editable parts yourself and submit your own completed circuit and test results.

Silicon diodes, constant-voltage-drop model: VD ≈ 0.7 V when ON, open circuit when OFF. Circuit (a): +10 V → 15 kΩ → node V; D2 from V to node B; D1 from ground to B; B → 5 kΩ → −10 V.

  1. Determine which diode(s) are ON and which are OFF.
  2. Find the node voltage V (with respect to ground).
  3. Find I (through D1, downward) and ID2 (through D2, downward).

Circuit Studio investigation

  1. Calculate first. Solve the questions above on a solution page, including assumptions and diode-state checks.
  2. Design. Plan the connections and diode orientations for the given two-supply circuit.
  3. Build. Start with the supplied unconnected parts. Wire the schematic yourself, run its DC test, then place components and jumpers on the virtual breadboard. Check wiring before powering it. Capture both completed circuits.
  4. Test and compare. At +10 V and −10 V, measure V and B relative to ground. Calculate both resistor currents from their voltage drops; use KCL at B to obtain the D1 current. Compare the measured diode polarities with your assumed states.
  5. Make one design choice. Change the top resistor from 15 kΩ to 10 kΩ. Predict the diode states and V before testing, then restore 15 kΩ.

Keep a compact table: setting | hand prediction | schematic result | breadboard reading. Record the diode model and explain model-related differences; do not change readings to match the 0.7 V approximation. For small-signal calculations use the stated 25 mV; the simulator may use a slightly different thermal voltage. A nonlinear diode model is needed to observe small voltage changes. If a constant-drop model fixes the voltage, report that limitation.

Credit: existing point values are unchanged. Support each answer with your calculations and the relevant circuit/test evidence. Final answers or starter images alone earn no credit.

Show your work: Show calculations and reasoning on solution pages or in notes. Final answers alone earn zero credit. For practical tasks include your completed schematic, breadboard, probe locations, readings with units, and a prediction-versus-test comparison. Use simulated supplies only. State any AI or automated-build assistance used; follow the instructor’s course policy.

Need wiring help? Open Hints and select Show next hint for the completed schematic. You can also enlarge the Original drawing in the sidebar. The editable starter still contains unconnected parts.
hints: Completed schematic reference: follow the connected diagram to wire your unconnected parts. Match every node, resistor value, diode bar (cathode), and supply polarity. Ground symbols represent the same reference node. Build the breadboard yourself, then check and test it. The supplied diagram is a hint, not evidence of your work.
Start by assuming both diodes ON: then B = −0.7 V and V = 0 V.
Check that the current into B through D₁ is positive.

questions.promptHtml:
Use this diagram as your wiring reference. Click the Original drawing in the sidebar to enlarge it. For build tasks, connect the editable parts yourself and submit your own completed circuit and test results.

For the regulator of Problem 3, a load RL = 1 kΩ is connected across vo.

  1. Find the new DC current through R.
  2. Estimate the new diode-string current and the new output voltage vo (small-signal model about the nominal point, n = 1, VT = 25 mV).
  3. Report vo for the no-load case.

Circuit Studio investigation

  1. Calculate first. Solve the questions above on a solution page, including assumptions and diode-state checks.
  2. Design. Design the load connection in parallel with the diode string, never in series. Start with the load disconnected.
  3. Build. Start with the supplied unconnected parts. Wire the schematic yourself, run its DC test, then place components and jumpers on the virtual breadboard. Check wiring before powering it. Capture both completed circuits.
  4. Test and compare. At 10 V, measure output voltage without the load and with RL=1 kΩ. On both representations record VO and calculate IR=(10−VO)/1 kΩ, IL=VO/RL, and ID=IR−IL. Compare the output change with your estimate.
  5. Make one design choice. Choose RL=2.2 kΩ or 470 Ω to reduce the output-voltage drop. Predict, test your choice, and restore RL=1 kΩ.

Keep a compact table: setting | hand prediction | schematic result | breadboard reading. Record the diode model and explain model-related differences; do not change readings to match the 0.7 V approximation. For small-signal calculations use the stated 25 mV; the simulator may use a slightly different thermal voltage. A nonlinear diode model is needed to observe small voltage changes. If a constant-drop model fixes the voltage, report that limitation.

questions.title: 8) Circuit Studio · Build and test a diode small-signal model
questions.promptHtml:
Use this diagram as your wiring reference. Click the Original drawing in the sidebar to enlarge it. For build tasks, connect the editable parts yourself and submit your own completed circuit and test results.

A small change around a DC bias point. Build a simple series circuit: a 5.00 V DC source, a 4.3 kΩ resistor, and a forward-biased diode. Connect the diode cathode (bar end) to ground and its anode to the resistor. Use the supplied diode model; for calculations use n = 1 and VT = 25.85 mV.

  1. Predict. Use VD ≈ 0.70 V to estimate IDQ = (5.00 − 0.70)/4300. Then calculate rd = nVT/IDQ. Sketch the incremental model with the diode replaced by rd.
  2. Build the schematic on the canvas and test it. The canvas contains only the unconnected voltage source, ground, R1 and diode. In Edit circuit, keep these four components and add the wires yourself. Wire V1+ → R1 → diode anode; connect the diode cathode and V1− to ground. Set V1 = 5.00 V and R1 = 4.3 kΩ; keep the supplied diode model (IS = 0.01 pA, n = 1). Run the DC test and record the diode voltage and current.
  3. Build the same circuit on the breadboard and test it. Open Build breadboard and place the components and jumpers yourself; Guide me and X-Ray are allowed. Check the wiring, then turn power on. Use the virtual multimeter with black on ground and red on the diode anode to measure VD,Q. Calculate IDQ = (5.00 − VD,Q)/4300. Compare with your canvas DC results.
